sections.text: A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you need it. You've already used one: main is the function every Rust program starts in. Functions can sit in any order in the file; a function's lines run only when it is called.
Make your own with fn, then call it by writing its name followed by ():
Functions can take inputs, called parameters. Each one needs a name and a type. i32 is Rust's everyday whole-number type:
Functions can also give back a result. Write -> and the result's type after the parameters. The last line, written without a semicolon, is the value given back:
Well-named functions make programs easier to read. area(4, 5) tells you what's happening without reading the maths inside.

exercise.prompt: Write a function called add that takes two i32 parameters, a and b, and gives back a + b as an i32. Then delete the // at the start of the line in main so it calls your function. The program should print: 7
hints: Look at the area function in the lesson. Yours has the same shape, with two inputs and one result.
Start with fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32. The last line, with no semicolon, is the value that is given back.
Between the curly braces write just a + b without a semicolon. Then remove the // in front of the println! line in main.

quiz.question: How do you run (call) a function named greet?
In fn square(n: i32) -> i32, what does -> i32 mean?
options: The function gives back a whole number

quiz.question: What is the value given back by a function?
options: Its last line without a semicolon
